To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the kinetic-energy flux due to saltating grains is strongly peaked above the bed during high winds; that this flux scales with the wind shear velocity to the fifth power; and that ventifact formation and erosion patterns are well explained by this model.

the kinetic-energy–flux distribution of wind-blown grains has a strong maximum.1–.5 m above a flat surface, and that this distribution is well modeled by an aerodynamic model that incorporates a realistic distribution of liftoff angles for saltating grains and a realistic distribution of particle sizes in the suspended load.

(1) erosion of objects of simple geometry by eolian saltation is well described by the kinetic-energy flux from the wind, and (2) erosion due to saltation is dominated by the impact of grains with velocities much higher than the mean velocity of the saltating cloud.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the physics of eolian sediment- transport processes.
the development of an eolian-sediment transport model, and the application of this model in the study of eolian erosion of natural and man-made objects.
the physics of wind erosion and the resulting geomorphology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the model is in excellent agreement with the data.
the model provides an excellent description of the physics of eolian transport and of the resulting erosion patterns, with the exception of some details concerning the role of suspended grains.
the wind erosion process is a complicated one, involving a variety of mechanisms, and that no one mechanism is dominant in all circumstances.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the model of eolian transport is sufficiently robust to permit the calculation of erosion profiles in a wide range of natural and man-made objects.
the kinetic-energy flux of saltating grains is the most important parameter in determining eolian erosion profiles.

the model of eolian saltation is robust enough to provide a reasonable first-order description of ventifaction and that the model is sufficiently detailed to permit a quantitative understanding of the processes involved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the kinetic energy of the wind is the key to understanding the erosional processes that shape the surface of the Earth.
ventifacts and eolian erosion profiles are a direct consequence of the physics of saltation.
the kinetic energy of particles entrained by the wind is not uniformly distributed in the flow, but is concentrated in a narrow region above the bed.
